family: A 2-DIN unit, split down to 1-DIN plus a pocket
one_liner: For cars with a double-height hole. The deck fills the top half and a pocket fills the bottom, which is how every 1-DIN radio has gone into a 2-DIN dash for thirty years.

price.v: £10–25 spares-or-repair, or £12–20 for a cage and pocket new
price.why: Broken 2-DIN units are cheap because a cracked touchscreen makes them worthless — and you were binning the screen anyway.

window_w_mm.why: You are building the top half yourself, so the window is whatever you cut. The donor supplies the cage and the surround, not the face.

chassis.v: steel, 2-DIN cage; you build a 1-DIN box inside it
chassis.why: The useful part is the CAGE and the trim ring, which are car-aperture-sized and hard to fabricate.

cage_included.v: yes, and it is the reason to buy one
cage_included.why: A 2-DIN cage plus a 1-DIN-and-pocket adapter is the whole point of this route.

buttons.v: whatever the donor had, often on a touchscreen instead
buttons.why: ⚠️ A touchscreen unit may have almost NO physical buttons. Count before relying on the fascia for six.

knob.v: often a single encoder, sometimes none
knob.why: Touchscreen-era units frequently have no knob at all, which is a poor start for a deck built around one.

display_tech.why: ⚠️ A backlit TFT has an inverter on the older ones. LED backlights do not. Check before probing.

why: It is the only sensible answer for a car with a 2-DIN aperture, and two cars in this project's vehicle list have one.
Cracked-screen 2-DIN units are worth nothing to anybody, and the screen is the part you were throwing away.
You get a 2-DIN cage and trim ring, which are the parts that are genuinely awkward to make and are sized to the car's hole.
The bottom half becomes real storage, which every owner of a small car wants anyway.
watch_out: ⚠️ You are building the 1-DIN box yourself — this route gives you the cage and the surround, not a ready-made chassis. Combine it with the fold-your-own or empty-pocket entries.
⚠️ Touchscreen units often have no usable buttons and no knob. Establish what physical controls exist before buying.
The 1-DIN half must sit at the TOP of the aperture, not the bottom, or the display ends up below the driver's sight line.
Older TFT backlights use an inverter. Not as lively as a VFD supply, still not something to probe blind.
steps: Confirm your car's aperture is actually 2-DIN — VEHICLES.md, then measure.
Buy the broken 2-DIN unit for its cage and trim ring, or buy those new.
Strip it: the screen, the mechanism and all the boards go.
Build or buy the 1-DIN box for the top half — see the fold-your-own and empty-pocket entries, which are the same job from here on.
Fit a 1-DIN storage pocket in the bottom half so the result looks intentional rather than gap-toothed.
⚠️ Mount the deck in the TOP half. A display below the centre console's midline is one you have to look down at.

models.name: Any 2-DIN CD/DVD receiver with a cracked screen
models.note: The cheapest source of a 2-DIN cage there is. The fault that makes it worthless is in the part you are removing.

models.name: Pioneer AVH- series
models.note: Common, and the cages and trim rings are well made.

models.name: Kenwood DDX / DNX series
models.note: As above. DNX are navigation units and go cheaper still once the maps are obsolete.

models.name: A 2-DIN cage and 1-DIN+pocket fascia, bought new
models.note: ✅ Skip the donor entirely. Under £20 for both, no teardown, no hazards — the same logic as the empty-pocket route one size up.

teardown.note: Off first, as on any unit. ⚠️ Older TFT backlights run from an inverter — do not probe it blind.
Comes off the front once the fascia is away. Sized to the car's aperture and one of the two reasons for this route.
You are not keeping this chassis, so the screws matter less than usual — but keep a few anyway.
Same caution as any disc unit: do not power it to test the laser.
Discharge the large electrolytics before binning.
⚠️ Unusual — on this route you do NOT keep the donor's box. It is the wrong height. You build a 1-DIN one.
The other reason for this route, and the part that is genuinely awkward to fabricate. It stays in the car.
